problems.title: Global dynamic slots require quadratic routing
problems.source_location: Current paper, Section 2.4, p. 6; author release src/models/soft_moe/soft_moe_with_dynamic_slots.py, lines 99–129 and 235–244.
claim: The dynamic hierarchy has linear routing complexity.
analysis: Let \(N\) be the input length, \(K\) the fixed group size, and \(E_1,S,E_2\) fixed expert/slot counts. The author implementation concatenates first-level slots into length \(L=\lceil N/K\rceil E_1S\). The next dynamic-slot layer pads to \(L'=E_2\lceil L/E_2\rceil\) and explicitly creates logits of shape \(B\times L'\times E_2\times(L'/E_2)\).

That tensor has \(B(L')^2\) entries, and its dot products cost \(\Theta(B(L')^2d)\). Thus global routing is quadratic in \(N\) at fixed grouping/width constants, despite constant-factor compression. For the stated first-stage settings, doubling \(N\) from \(110592\) to \(221184\) doubles global length from \(864\) to \(1728\), and multiplies logits entries from \(746496\) to \(2985984\). These are shape counts, not total GPU-memory measurements.
result: The strict linear-scaling explanation does not describe the author-released global routing. Small-input speed or memory benefits can still be real.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.
repair: Report the full grouped/global complexity. Fixed global slot count \(Q\) would give \(O(BLQd)\) routing, but that changes the architecture and would need new training.
problems.impact_rationale: The central linear-routing scalability explanation conflicts with an explicit quadratic tensor lower bound for the released architecture. This substantial complexity error meets Major even without claiming failure of small-input experiments.
problems.existing_correction_status: Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The two-stage algorithm differs from the execution graph
claim: The published two-stage equations describe the released execution graph.
analysis: The current paper uses learned slot embeddings and a group softmax router, whereas HierarchicalDynamicSlotsSoftMoE.forward generates embeddings from group means, uses learned scalar expert gates and a sigmoid group gate, and applies DynamicSlotsSoftMoE to all concatenated group slots. Under a pointwise interpretation of the printed FFNs, reshape followed by channel FFNs cannot create cross-group dependence: \(\partial y_g/\partial x_h=0\) for distinct groups. A matrix-valued FFN could instead mix tokens, so this is a conditional illustration of incomplete specification, not proof that every interpretation is local. The actual source performs global dispatch and has the quadratic routing counted above; the Mamba branch also supplies long-range dependence.
result: The bounded local discrepancy or counterexample is supported; no change in published benchmark scores is quantified.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.
repair: Reconcile the specific equation, reported quantity or source contract described above. Corrected full-experiment results remain unverified.
problems.impact_rationale: This establishes the stated local correction or limitation. A consequential failure of the paper's central result has not been demonstrated.

problems.title: Slot ablation does not keep parameters and memory fixed
claim: Changing slot count holds parameters and memory fixed.
analysis: The current slot projection is a bias-free linear map from \(d\) to \(dE_1S\), containing \(d^2E_1S\) weights. With the four stated stage widths and expert counts and two repetitions per stage, these projections alone contain \(5769216S\) weights. Changing \(S=4\) to \(S=8\) therefore adds \(23076864\) parameters. The global routing length is also proportional to \(S\), so its array scales quadratically with \(S\). This contradicts the current p. 9 statement that the slot variations keep parameters and GPU memory constant; it does not replace a measured peak-memory comparison.
result: The bounded local discrepancy or counterexample is supported; no change in published benchmark scores is quantified.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.

problems.title: Macro-average summaries conflict with their definition
claim: mDSC and mHD95 use the stated macro-average formulas.
analysis: Equation (19) explicitly gives equal weight to classes. In current Table 12, Hermes lists \[79.3,74.2,90.7,87.6,87.1,88.8,84.7\]; their mean is \(84.6286\%\), while the displayed mDSC is \(86.5\%\). Entry rounding cannot explain the \(1.8714\)-point difference. In Table 22, the seven foreground means for \(S=4\) and \(S=8\) are \(85.7714\%\) and \(85.9429\%\), while their displayed aggregates \(87.5\%\) and \(87.4\%\) reverse this order. An unreported background class could explain some FeTA values, but is not established. Different case/class aggregation or empty-mask handling requires a stated alternative definition; unrounded case outputs are needed to select final numbers.

analysis: Current Table 3 gives SegMamba FeTA mDSC/mHD95 as \(85.9/3.5\), whereas Table 12 gives \(86.5/5.8\). problems.title: Decoder and resource descriptions leave limited reproducibility gaps
problems.source_location: Current paper, Eq. (17) and final prediction description, p. 6; DyT Table 8, p. 9; timing definition, Eq. (27), p. 20; author release src/models/MambaHoME.py.
claim: The decoder restores full resolution and the resource summaries describe the implemented measurements.
analysis: The printed \(I-1\) decoder stages start from a downsampled stem; the final prediction description leaves the final restoration operation implicit. The author model includes additional decoding, so no wrong output size is established. Table 8 gives default DyT FeTA mDSC \(87.4\), versus \(87.5\) in other default tables; different runs or rounding may account for this small difference. Hardware and timing definitions are supplied, but complete run-specific volumes, synchronization and memory-reset details are not linked to every result. The coarse displayed speed ratios alone do not refute the approximate prose percentage.
result: These are unresolved specification/run-provenance limits. The current code includes final decoding; no decoder-size failure or false measured speedup is established.
